title: A healing and a mercy
hook: We send down in the Qur'an what is a healing and a mercy (17:82)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the unseen, and your line: faith in the unseen. Did you leave one guess about the future where it belongs? Today, what the book says it does for the one who hears it. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

A desert camp, somewhere in Arabia. A small band of the Prophet's companions has stopped near a tribe that won't host them. That night the tribe's chief is stung by a scorpion, and nothing they try helps. Someone comes over: does any of you know a cure? One companion says he does. He sits by the chief and recites the Fatiha over him, again and again, blowing lightly as he goes. The hadith, in al-Bukhari, says the chief got up as if he'd been freed from a rope.

When the companions got back to Medina and told the Prophet ﷺ, he asked the reciter: how did you know it was a ruqyah, a recitation for healing? He approved what they'd done. That story sits behind a word the Qur'an uses about itself. Surah seventeen, verse eighty-two, in Pickthall's translation: "And We reveal of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for believers." The word for healing is shifa'. Many Muslim families name a daughter Shifa. Elsewhere the Qur'an calls itself a healing for what is in the breasts, the hearts, in surah ten, and a guidance and a healing in surah forty-one. Notice what kind of healing is named most. Commentators say the first sickness in view is in the heart: doubt, fear, grief, a restless mind. The book is a mercy for that. Many also hold, from hadith like the scorpion story, that its recitation can be a means of healing for the body. And Islamic teaching doesn't set this against medicine. A hadith in al-Bukhari says Allah has not sent down a disease without sending down a cure for it. Muslim physicians built hospitals and wrote medical books for centuries, and many prayed and recited as well. So shifa' comes in two hands at once. A doctor's prescription in one. A verse in the other. Neither has to cancel the other out. On a low day, the second hand is the one people sometimes forget they have.
screen: `MEDICINE IN ONE HAND, A VERSE IN THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: read a verse when you're low. You don't have to be low right now. Practice for the day you are. Sit and breathe slowly. Bring to mind a short verse or passage you know, the Fatiha, or any line from this year that stayed with you. If none comes, simply hold the words a healing and a mercy. Say it slowly, inside or aloud, three times, letting each word take a full breath. Notice whether anything in your chest loosens even a little. The bell holds the time.
Shifa'. Healing. The Qur'an calls itself a healing and a mercy for believers, first for the heart, and recited, many hold, for the body too. Today's word.
Your line: a healing. Today, choose one verse or line and keep it somewhere you'll see it, a note on your phone or a slip in your wallet, for the next low moment. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the Fatiha, the last two surahs and other verses over someone who is ill (ruqyah), while also seeking medical treatment, which a well-known hadith encourages.
